points: Show how you create structure when nobody gives you one
Steps: ask who it is for, write down what success looks like, pick the smallest thing to test
Say what you assumed, and how you checked it

sections.label: Example
points: S: a club asked me to "make the event app better" with no brief
A: interviewed five members, found check-in was the pain, and wrote a one-line goal: check-in under 30 seconds
A: built a QR check-in as the smallest test and timed it at the next event
R: average check-in dropped from 2 minutes to 25 seconds; the club adopted it for every event

tip: Product work starts vague. They want to see you turn a fuzzy ask into a goal, a test and a number.
failureMode: Waiting to be told what to do, or jumping into building before agreeing what success means.

question: Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete information.

sections.label: How to answer
points: Name what you knew, what you did not, and how you decided anyway
Show you sized the risk: how bad if wrong, how easy to undo
Show you went back and checked the result

sections.label: Example
points: S: we had two days to pick a topic for a hackathon demo and no user data
A: listed what we could not know, chose the option that was cheap to change, and set a checkpoint after day one
A: asked three target users a single question to cut the biggest unknown
R: the checkpoint caught a flaw early; we switched on day two without losing the demo

tip: Real product decisions never have full data. They look for a reversible-or-not call and a plan to learn fast.
failureMode: Saying you waited for more data, or claiming you decided on gut with no way to check.

question: Tell me about a time you took ownership of something outside your job.

sections.label: How to answer
points: Pick a gap nobody owned that hurt the team
Show you did it without being asked, and without dropping your own work
Quantify what changed

sections.label: Example
points: S: our society kept missing sponsor follow-ups because nobody tracked them
A: built a shared sheet with owner, date and status for every sponsor, and ran a five-minute weekly check
A: handed it to a junior member after two months with a one-page guide
R: follow-ups on time went from about half to nearly all; we closed two more sponsors that term

tip: Product managers own outcomes without a manual. They look for initiative that stays small and leaves something behind.
failureMode: Describing a heroic one-off with no lasting change, or taking credit for what the team did.

question: Tell me about a time you got people to do something without being their manager.

sections.label: How to answer
points: Product managers have no direct reports, so this is the core skill
Show you found what the other person cared about and linked the ask to it
Name the result and the relationship afterwards

sections.label: Example
points: S: I needed two developers on a college project to fix a bug that was not in their tasks
A: showed them it blocked the demo they were presenting, and offered to test every fix myself
A: split it into two small tickets so each could finish in an hour
R: both fixed it that evening; they came to me for the next planning round

tip: This is the product manager job in one question. They listen for motive and framing, not for pressure or favours.
failureMode: Saying you escalated to someone senior, or that you asked nicely until they agreed.

question: Tell me about a time you said no to something.

sections.label: How to answer
points: Show you said no to protect a goal, not to avoid work
Give the reason, offer an alternative, and keep the relationship
It is stronger if the person later agreed you were right

sections.label: Example
points: S: a teammate asked me to add five features the week before submission
A: showed that each added risk to the one feature judges would score, and ranked them by impact
A: kept one, moved the rest to a "next version" list with owners
R: we submitted on time with a stable demo; the list became our roadmap

tip: Prioritisation is saying no with a reason. They check that your no comes from a goal, not from comfort.
failureMode: A flat refusal with no reason and no alternative, or a story where you gave in.

question: Why do you want to join this company?

sections.label: How to answer
points: Name one product decision of theirs you admire, and why
Say what you would want to work on, and what you bring to it
Be specific — one detail only they would have

sections.label: Example
points: I use [product] daily and noticed [specific choice], which tells me you put [value] ahead of [shortcut]
On [project] I worked on a similar problem: [one line]
I want to learn [skill] from a team that ships to millions of people, and give back [strength]

tip: They test whether you did your homework and whether you can talk about their product like an owner.
failureMode: A generic answer that fits any company: big brand, great culture, lots of learning.

question: What are your strengths and your biggest weakness?

sections.label: How to answer
points: Strengths: pick two that a product manager needs, and prove each with a one-line example
Weakness: a real one that is not a core skill, and say what you are doing about it
Never use a disguised strength such as "I work too hard"

sections.label: Example
points: Strength: structure — I break a vague problem into parts; I did that for [project]
Strength: listening — I ask one more question before proposing a fix
Weakness: I used to over-polish before sharing; now I share a rough version on day one and fix what people point at

tip: Self-awareness is the point. They want evidence you notice your own gaps and act on them.
failureMode: Giving a fake weakness, or naming one that rules you out of the role, with no sign you are working on it.

question: How would you improve a UPI payments app for first-time users?

sections.label: Framework
points: Clarify the goal and who it is for
Pick one user segment and one problem
Propose one solution, not five
Name the metrics, and one guardrail

sections.label: Answer
points: Goal: more first-time users complete their first payment within a day
Segment: someone with a first smartphone who is nervous about losing money
Problem: the drop-off sits at linking the bank and setting the UPI PIN, which needs debit card details most people do not have in hand
Solution: a guided setup that says up front what you need ("keep your debit card ready"), explains each step in the local language, and ends with a small practice payment to a trusted merchant
Metrics: setup completion rate, first payment within 24 hours, support contacts per 100 setups
Guardrail: scam and wrong-recipient reports — easy setup must not make fraud easier

tip: Strong answers find the step where people fall off, instead of adding features to the home screen.
failureMode: Redesigning the home screen or adding rewards, when the real problem is the first-time setup.

question: How would you improve YouTube for people who use it to learn?

sections.label: Framework
points: Clarify the goal and who it is for
Pick one user segment and one problem
Propose one solution, not five
Name the metrics, and one guardrail

sections.label: Answer
points: Goal: more learners finish what they start, and come back
Segment: students preparing for an exam or picking up a skill
Problem: the recommendations pull them to unrelated videos, and there is no path, notes or progress
Solution: a "Learning mode" that turns a playlist into a course — progress bar, chapter notes, and no recommendations sidebar until the lesson ends
Metrics: course completion rate, days per week a learner returns
Guardrail: total watch time and creator revenue — fewer detours is a trade-off to measure, not ignore

tip: Say who loses out. A good answer names the business cost of your idea and measures it.
failureMode: Proposing features for everyone on the platform instead of one segment with a clear problem.

question: Design a quick-commerce grocery app for a tier-2 city.

sections.label: Framework
points: Clarify the goal and who it is for
Pick one user segment and one problem
Propose one solution, not five
Name the metrics, and one guardrail

sections.label: Answer
points: Goal: a profitable launch in one city, not a copy of the metro model
Segment: families ordering weekly staples, not 10-minute snacks
Constraints: lower order value, thin delivery density, addresses by landmark, preference for cash on delivery, regional language
Solution: scheduled delivery slots instead of 10 minutes, a curated 500-item range of staples, pin-on-map plus a call to the rider, cash on delivery
Metrics: orders per rider per hour, repeat orders in four weeks, cost per delivery
Question the premise: speed may not be what this city values

tip: They want to see you adapt a model to a market, not paste it. Start from what is different there.
failureMode: Copying the metro 10-minute promise without checking if delivery density can pay for it.

question: How would you improve WhatsApp for small businesses?

sections.label: Framework
points: Clarify the goal and who it is for
Pick one user segment and one problem
Propose one solution, not five
Name the metrics, and one guardrail

sections.label: Answer
points: Goal: sellers run more of their business inside WhatsApp
Segment: a home-run seller who takes repeat orders over chat
Problem: orders are buried in chat threads, so they get lost, forgotten or mis-added
Solution: an order inbox that turns a chat into an order with items, amount and status, plus a repeat-order reminder for regular customers
Metrics: orders handled per seller per week, repeat orders per customer
Guardrail: spam reports and blocks — reminders must not annoy buyers

tip: The best answers keep the product simple for a seller with no staff and a phone in one hand.
failureMode: Adding a full e-commerce suite that a one-person seller will never learn.

question: How would you improve train ticket booking in India?

sections.label: Framework
points: Clarify the goal and who it is for
Pick one user segment and one problem
Propose one solution, not five
Name the metrics, and one guardrail

sections.label: Answer
points: Goal: more travellers leave with a confirmed seat and less stress
Segment: occasional travellers booking when seats are scarce
Problem: a waitlisted ticket gives no sense of whether it will confirm, and a failed payment at peak loses the seat
Solution: show a confirmation chance for waitlisted tickets, and offer nearby dates, trains or stations that are likely to confirm
Metrics: confirmed-booking rate, time to book, payment failure rate
Guardrail: accuracy of the confirmation chance — a wrong promise breaks trust

tip: Honest uncertainty is the product here. Showing a probability beats hiding the waitlist.
failureMode: Redesigning screens and colours while the real pain is the uncertainty of the waitlist.

question: Design an alarm clock for people who cannot wake up.

sections.label: Framework
points: Clarify the goal and who it is for
Pick one user segment and one problem
Propose one solution, not five
Name the metrics, and one guardrail

sections.label: Answer
points: Goal: the user is awake, not only silenced
Segment: heavy sleepers who dismiss the alarm half-asleep
Problem: turning it off is too easy and needs no thought
Solution: make the dismissal need effort that wakes you — scan a code in another room, do a short puzzle, or step out of bed — and raise the volume gently while it waits
Metrics: share of users awake 10 minutes after the alarm, snooze count, 30-day retention
Guardrail: uninstalls and one-star reviews — an annoying alarm gets deleted

tip: Define success as "awake", then design for it. Many candidates stop at louder alarms.
failureMode: Making the alarm louder, which wakes the neighbours and does not wake the user.

question: Design a fitness app for people who have never exercised regularly.

sections.label: Framework
points: Clarify the goal and who it is for
Pick one user segment and one problem
Propose one solution, not five
Name the metrics, and one guardrail

sections.label: Answer
points: Goal: a beginner is still exercising after four weeks
Segment: a first-time gym-goer or home-workout starter
Problem: they do not know what to do, and most quit within three weeks
Solution: three sessions a week of 20 minutes that adapt to what you finished, with one clear task each day and no choice overload
Metrics: week-4 retention, sessions completed per week
Guardrail: injury reports and feedback that sessions are too hard

tip: Retention is the whole game for beginners. Design the first month, not the feature list.
failureMode: Building a huge workout library for people who need one plan.

question: Design an elevator for a hospital.

sections.label: Framework
points: Clarify who uses it: patients on beds and wheelchairs, staff, visitors
List what each needs, then rank by urgency
Design for the most critical user first
Name how you would measure it

sections.label: Answer
points: Priority: a key-call mode that sends the lift straight to a floor for stretchers and emergencies
Separate clinical lifts from visitor lifts so beds never wait in a crowd
Wide doors, controls at bed height, touchless buttons, floor and department shown in large type and voice
Metrics: wait time for emergency calls, time per bed transfer between floors
Guardrail: visitor wait time — protecting emergencies must not strand everyone else

tip: Hardware questions test whether you start with users and rank their needs, not with gadgets.
failureMode: Listing gadgets before deciding who the primary user is.

question: How would you improve LinkedIn for students and freshers?

sections.label: Framework
points: Clarify the goal and who it is for
Pick one user segment and one problem
Propose one solution, not five
Name the metrics, and one guardrail

sections.label: Answer
points: Goal: more freshers get a recruiter message within 30 days of joining
Segment: final-year students with projects but no job history
Problem: profiles are built around work experience, so freshers look empty and recruiters filter them out
Solution: a projects-first profile with proof of work, plus a one-tap request for a referral from alumni at a target company
Metrics: recruiter messages per fresher, referral requests accepted
Guardrail: alumni spam reports — referral requests must not flood the same people

tip: Pick the group with the clearest unmet need. Freshers are an easy segment to defend with data.
failureMode: Saying "add more features for students" with no specific problem.

question: How would you price a new subscription product?

sections.label: Framework
points: Three lenses: what it costs us, what competitors charge, what it is worth to the user
Value wins; cost sets the floor; competitors set the range

sections.label: Answer
points: Floor: cost to serve one user per month, plus a margin
Range: what the two closest alternatives charge
Value: ask target users what is too cheap and too expensive, and test two price points on the paywall
For students in India: a low monthly price, a discounted annual plan, and a free tier that proves value first
Watch: conversion to paid, 3-month retention, refund rate

tip: Show you test price instead of guessing it. A price is a hypothesis.
failureMode: Picking a number from a competitor with no reason, or only adding a margin to cost.

question: Should a food delivery app launch in a new city?

sections.label: Framework
points: Market: how many people order, and what they pay
Competition: who is already there
Economics: can orders per day cover riders and kitchens
Risk: how cheaply can we test it

sections.label: Answer
points: Size the city: population, share with smartphones, share who order out
Check supply: enough restaurants within delivery range of dense areas
Break-even: orders per rider per hour needed to pay for delivery
Pilot two dense zones first; expand only if orders per rider clear break-even for four weeks
Decision rule set before launch: the number that makes us stop

tip: A decision rule set in advance shows discipline. Interviewers want a yes or no with the number that flips it.
failureMode: Saying "it depends" and never naming the number that decides it.

question: Should we build our own payments feature or buy one from a vendor?

sections.label: Framework
points: Is this what makes us different, or a utility
Compare time, cost over three years, control and risk

sections.label: Answer
points: If it is a utility, buy: payments are heavily regulated and slow to build well
Time: a vendor ships in weeks; building takes quarters
Cost: add vendor fees against the team you would hire, over three years
Risk: lock-in, data access, compliance on both sides
Recommendation: buy now, keep the integration thin so we can swap later; revisit build when volume makes fees the bigger cost

tip: They want a stated recommendation with the trigger that changes it.
failureMode: Listing pros and cons with no recommendation.

question: How do you compete with a free product?

sections.label: Framework
points: Do not fight on price
Find what free cannot do, and who needs that

sections.label: Answer
points: Name the gap: reliability, support, depth, integration, or trust with data
Pick the segment that pays for that gap, such as teams or professionals
Offer a free tier that proves the value, then charge where cost to serve rises
Use the free product as the top of the funnel: import from it, integrate with it
Metric: paid conversion in the target segment, not total users

tip: A free competitor is a segmentation problem. The answer is who it fails.
failureMode: Cutting your price toward zero or listing features the free product also has.

question: A global app is launching in India. What do you change?

sections.label: Framework
points: Payments, language, devices, price, trust
Choose the two that decide whether anyone gets past onboarding

sections.label: Answer
points: Payments: UPI first, and cash on delivery where it is a physical product; payment data must be stored in India under RBI rules
Language: Hindi and the big regional languages in the first flow, not buried in settings
Devices: low-end Android phones, small app size, works on a weak network
Price: smaller price points and short plans such as weekly or daily
Trust: WhatsApp-style support and clear refund promises

tip: The best answers rank the changes by what blocks a new user, instead of listing every difference.
failureMode: A list of generic points like "understand the culture" with no specific change.

question: Subscriber churn is rising. What is your strategy?

sections.label: Framework
points: Split churn into voluntary and failed-payment churn
Find when it happens, then why

sections.label: Answer
points: Cohort view: do users leave in month one (onboarding), or later (value faded)
Failed payments: retry sensibly and remind users before the card expires — this is often a quick win
Month-one churn: fix onboarding so the first week shows the core value
Later churn: build habit hooks, and offer a pause instead of a cancel
Add an annual plan for the segment that stays; offer win-back messages with a reason to return
Success: 3-month retention up, involuntary churn down

tip: Splitting churn into types is the answer. Each type has a different fix.
failureMode: Proposing discounts for everyone before finding why people leave.

question: How do you decide what not to build?

sections.label: Framework
points: Tie every idea to the current goal
Score the rest and say no with a reason

sections.label: Answer
points: Ask: which goal does this move this quarter? No answer, no build
Score with a simple model such as RICE, so the call is visible
Say no in one sentence with the reason, and offer a smaller alternative
Keep a "not now" list with a date to revisit, so no is not forever
Check yourself: what did we cut last quarter, and did we miss it?

tip: Great product managers are known for what they cut. Tell a story where saying no helped.
failureMode: Saying you never say no, or that you ship everything stakeholders ask for.

question: Plan the go-to-market for a new budgeting app for college students.

sections.label: Framework
points: Who first, which channel, what hook, how we measure
Start narrow: one segment in one place

sections.label: Answer
points: Segment: students living away from home with a monthly allowance
Hook: split shared costs with roommates over UPI — a reason to invite friends
Channel: campus ambassadors, hostel WhatsApp groups, short videos by student creators
Pricing: free at launch; charge later for extras such as reports
Pilot at three campuses for a month
Metrics: activation (first expense logged in 24 hours), invites per user, week-4 retention

tip: Narrow beats broad. A launch to three campuses with a number to hit is a plan.
failureMode: "Launch everywhere with ads" and no first segment.

question: What North Star metric would you pick for a food delivery app?

sections.label: Framework
points: The North Star is the one number that tracks value delivered to users
Test it: if it rises, is the business healthier?

sections.label: Answer
points: Candidates: orders, weekly active orderers, orders per user per month
Pick weekly orders from repeat customers: it shows habit and value, and revenue follows
Not revenue alone: discounts can buy it without value
Inputs that move it: new users, repeat rate, restaurant availability, delivery time
Guardrails: delivery time, order cancellations, refund rate

tip: Explain why you rejected the obvious option. That shows judgement.
failureMode: Picking revenue or downloads without checking it reflects value to users.

question: Your A/B test shows no difference between the versions. What do you do?

sections.label: Framework
points: Was the test able to find a difference at all?
Then decide on the other evidence

sections.label: Answer
points: Check power: did we have enough users for the effect we cared about? If not, the test says nothing
Look at guardrail metrics and segments, but treat a segment win as an idea to test, not a result
If it is truly flat, ship the simpler or cheaper version, or drop the change
Write down what we learned so the next test starts smarter

tip: A flat result is information. Interviewers check you do not hunt for a winner in the noise.
failureMode: Slicing the data until some segment shows a win and shipping on it.

question: How do you decide how long to run an A/B test and how many users you need?

sections.label: Framework
points: Decide before you start, not after you look

sections.label: Answer
points: Set the smallest improvement worth detecting, the current baseline, a 5% significance level and 80% power
Those four numbers give the sample size; divide by daily traffic to get days
Run full weeks so weekday and weekend behaviour both show up
Do not stop early because the number looks good; peeking inflates false wins
Pre-define the one success metric and the guardrails

tip: You do not need the formula. You need to know what goes into it and why peeking is a problem.
failureMode: Stopping the test the day the result turns positive.

question: Checkout conversion is up 8% but revenue per user is down. What happened?

sections.label: Framework
points: Revenue per user = orders × order value
Find which part moved

sections.label: Answer
points: Possible cause: easier checkout, but basket size fell because we removed the upsell step
Possible cause: a discount drove more small orders from price-sensitive users
Possible cause: mix change: more new users who spend less than regulars
Check: split by new and existing users, by order value band, and by channel
Decide on profit and lifetime value, not on conversion alone

tip: Break a metric into parts before you theorise. Two numbers moving apart is a mix or a trade-off.
failureMode: Celebrating conversion alone, or guessing one cause without splitting the data.

question: How would you define activation for a language-learning app?

sections.label: Framework
points: Activation is the first moment the user gets real value
Find the action that best predicts they stay

sections.label: Answer
points: Candidate: complete the first lesson
Better: complete two lessons across two days — it signals a habit
Check it with data: which early action best separates users who are still active in week four
Track the share of new users who reach it within seven days
Guardrail: do not shape onboarding so it forces the action and annoys users

tip: Show that you would find the activation event from retention data, not from opinion.
failureMode: Defining activation as signing up or installing.

question: You are launching a faster checkout. What guardrail metrics do you set?

sections.label: Framework
points: Primary: checkout conversion
Guardrails: what must not get worse

sections.label: Answer
points: Payment failure rate and error rate
Refunds and order cancellations: speed must not cause mistakes
Average order value, if the new flow drops an upsell step
Fraud rate, if you removed a verification step
Page load time and support tickets about checkout

tip: Guardrails show maturity. Always say what you will do if one trips.
failureMode: Naming only the metric you hope to improve.

question: Users say they want a feature, but the usage data says they would not use it. What do you do?

sections.label: Framework
points: What people say and what they do often differ
Test behaviour before you build

sections.label: Answer
points: Trust behaviour for what people do; use interviews for why they do it
Ask what problem sits behind the request
Run a cheap test: a fake button, a waitlist, or a manual version
If people click and then use it, build it; if not, you saved the cost
Tell the people who asked what you learned

tip: A cheap test beats an argument. They like seeing a fake-door or manual version.
failureMode: Building the requested feature because customers asked loudly.

question: How do you measure a brand-new feature that has no baseline?

sections.label: Framework
points: No baseline means create one
Compare against a holdout or a proxy

sections.label: Answer
points: Define the job it does and the action that shows it worked
Hold back a small share of users who do not get it, and compare
If you cannot hold back, compare against a similar feature or the time before launch
Start with usage and repeat use, then move to the business metric
Set a target before launch so success is not decided after

tip: Say how you would create a comparison group. That is the whole answer.
failureMode: Reporting raw usage numbers with nothing to compare them to.

question: Explain what an API is to a non-technical stakeholder.

sections.label: Answer
points: Think of a restaurant: you (the app) tell the waiter (the API) what you want, and the kitchen (another system) prepares it
The menu is the list of things you are allowed to ask for
You never walk into the kitchen; the API controls what you can request and what you get back
Example: a weather app asks a weather service for today's forecast through its API
Why it matters to a product manager: every API has limits, costs and downtime that become your product's limits

tip: Plain language with one example is the test. Then add why it matters for the product.
failureMode: Defining an API with more jargon, such as "an interface that exposes endpoints".

question: How do you choose between SQL and NoSQL for a new product?

sections.label: Framework
points: Ask what the data looks like and how it is used

sections.label: Answer
points: SQL (relational): structured data with relationships that must stay consistent, such as orders and payments; easy reporting
NoSQL (document, key-value): flexible shapes, huge write volume, simple lookups, such as chat messages or activity feeds
Many products use both: SQL for the core records, NoSQL for high-volume side data
A product manager should ask: how will this data be queried, and what happens if two writes clash
Default for a new product: start relational unless you have a clear reason

tip: You do not pick the database. You ask the questions that lead the team to the right one.
failureMode: Saying NoSQL is always better because it scales.

question: What happens when you type a web address and press enter?

sections.label: Framework
points: Follow the request out and back

sections.label: Answer
points: The browser asks DNS to turn the name into a server address
It opens a secure connection to that server
It sends a request; the server may check a cache, run application code and read a database
The server sends back HTML; the browser then fetches styles, scripts and images
The browser draws the page; slow steps along the way are what users feel as lag
Product link: each step is a place a page can be slow or fail

tip: Follow one request end to end. Mentioning where it can fail shows product thinking.
failureMode: Stopping at "the server sends the page" with no detail on the steps between.

question: An engineer says a feature will take six weeks. How do you respond?

sections.label: Framework
points: Understand the estimate, then negotiate scope, not time

sections.label: Answer
points: Ask what is in the six weeks: design, build, test, rollout
Ask what the biggest unknowns and risks are
Ask what the smallest useful version would take and what it leaves out
Check dependencies on other teams or vendors
Never push the number down; cut scope or add a milestone instead
Agree a checkpoint at week two to catch slippage early

tip: Engineers trust product managers who ask about risk and offer scope, not pressure.
failureMode: Asking "can it be done faster?" with no change to scope.

question: How do you decide between paying down tech debt and shipping new features?

sections.label: Framework
points: Put a cost on the debt, then compare it with feature value

sections.label: Answer
points: Ask engineering what the debt costs: slower releases, incidents, hours lost per sprint
Link it to a business outcome: "every feature takes 30% longer" is a number leaders understand
Fix debt that blocks the next quarter's goals first
Reserve a fixed share of every sprint, 15–20% is a common start, so it is never a negotiation
Report back what the debt work unlocked

tip: Treat tech debt as a business cost. A fixed share of every sprint avoids the yearly argument.
failureMode: Saying features always come first, or that engineers decide on debt alone.

question: What is caching, and when does it cause a product problem?

sections.label: Framework
points: Caching keeps a copy of data close so it loads faster

sections.label: Answer
points: A cache stores answers to repeated requests, so the system does less work
Benefit: faster pages and lower server cost
Risk: the copy can be stale — a price, a stock count or a profile photo that has already changed
Example: a product shows "in stock" from a cached page while the last unit is sold
Product question: how stale can this data be? Payments and stock: seconds. A trending list: minutes
Ask engineering for the refresh time of each important number

tip: Staleness is the product risk. Name an example where it hurts the user.
failureMode: Explaining caching as "making things faster" with no mention of stale data.

question: What would you do in your first 30 days as a product manager?

sections.label: Answer
points: Week 1: listen. Meet engineers, design, support and sales; ask what hurts and what they would change
Week 2: use the product like a new user and read the last quarter of data and feedback
Week 3: write down the top three problems, with evidence, and share them with your manager
Week 4: pick one small, visible improvement and ship it
Throughout: learn the metrics the team is judged on

tip: A calm, listening-first plan beats a big vision. A small win in week four earns trust.
failureMode: Promising a new strategy or a redesign before you have listened to anyone.

question: How do you work with engineers day to day?

sections.label: Answer
points: Share the problem and the reason, before the solution
Bring them in early, while options are still open
Write a clear, short spec and answer questions fast
Respect their estimates; negotiate scope, not time
Protect them from changing priorities mid-sprint
Say thank you in public and take the blame in public

tip: Engineers are your main partners. They are testing whether you treat them as thinkers or as builders on call.
failureMode: Describing engineers as people you hand requirements to.

question: What goes into a product requirements document, and how long should it be?

sections.label: Answer
points: The problem and who has it, with evidence
The goal and the success metric
The scope: what is in, and what is explicitly out
The user flow or a rough design
Open questions, risks and dependencies
Keep it to one or two pages; if it is longer, split the work

tip: Short and clear wins. The document exists so people can question it, not so it looks thorough.
failureMode: Writing a long document nobody reads, with no stated success metric.

question: What is an MVP, and how do you decide what goes in it?

sections.label: Answer
points: The smallest version that tests your riskiest assumption with real users
Not a bad product; a focused one
Find the riskiest assumption first, such as "people will pay" or "people will come back"
Include only what is needed to test that assumption
Set the result that counts as success before you build
Example: a manual service run on WhatsApp before building an app

tip: Tie the MVP to an assumption and a result. That separates it from "version one".
failureMode: Calling a half-built product with every feature an MVP.

question: How would you do user research with no budget?

sections.label: Answer
points: Talk to five real users; five conversations find most big problems
Recruit from where users already are: communities, WhatsApp groups, your own network
Ask about past behaviour, such as "tell me about the last time you…", not about opinions on your idea
Watch someone use the product or a competitor and note where they stall
Read support tickets, app reviews and forum posts for free evidence
Write what you learned in three lines and share it with the team

tip: Show that research is a habit, not a budget. Ask about the past, not the future.
failureMode: Asking friends whether they like your idea.
